topic.angle: The railway worker who survived an iron rod through the head

card.title: The man who survived an iron rod

panels.text: Vermont, 13 September 1848. Phineas Gage, a railroad construction foreman, is packing explosive powder into a rock with an iron bar.
The powder explodes. The bar, about 3 feet 7 inches long and weighing around 6 kg, shoots through his left cheek and out of the top of his skull.
Gage is awake within minutes and speaks. He survives, and lives for another twelve years.
The twist: stories say the accident turned him into a different person. Later research suggests those accounts were exaggerated, and he went back to work, driving horses in Chile.

probes.question: True or false: Phineas Gage died soon after his accident.

image_brief.show: The daguerreotype portrait of Phineas Gage holding his tamping iron, or a railroad construction scene

claims.claim: Phineas Gage was a railroad construction foreman; accident in Vermont on 13 September 1848.
claims.quote: blasting foreman directing a work gang that was preparing a railroad roadbed
claims.note: Article text gives September 13, 1848 near Cavendish, Vermont (tamping iron inscription says 14th).

claims.claim: He was packing explosive powder into a rock with an iron bar.
claims.note: Source says the iron packs sand, clay or other inert material above the powder. Suggested: "packing a blasting hole with an iron tamping bar".

claims.claim: Bar about 3 feet 7 inches long, around 6 kg.
claims.quote: 3 feet 7 inches (1.1 m) long and 13¼ pounds (6.0 kg)

claims.claim: The bar went through his left cheek and out the top of his skull.
claims.note: Exit through top of skull also stated per fetch summary.

claims.claim: He spoke within minutes of the accident.
claims.note: Card says "awake within minutes"; source supports speaking within minutes; he had brief convulsions first.

claims.claim: He survived and lived about twelve years more.
claims.quote: died on May 21, 1860, at age 36, about 12 years after the accident

claims.claim: Accounts of personality change were exaggerated.
He later worked driving horses in Chile.
claims.quote: long-distance stagecoach driver on the Valparaiso-Santiago route
claims.note: Source: from 1852, stagecoaches pulled by six horses in Chile. Card says "went back to work" - fine.

claims.claim: Probe: Gage did not die soon after the accident (false).
Probe: an iron tamping bar passed through his skull.
